ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Acute worsening of a very itchy, sore, red, dry rash
- Onset/duration: Past few days; progressively worse
- Location/distribution: Chest, hands, and arms; worst in antecubital fossae (inside of elbows)
- Character: Very pruritic, dry; cracked skin; no weeping/exudate; no noted thickening/lichenification; patient reports no visible scratch marks
- Aggravating/alleviating factors: No change in topical regimen; OTC hydrocortisone tried without relief; prior OTC antihistamine (likely cetirizine) not helpful; continues emollients (Diprobase) and Dermol wash
- Associated symptoms: Denies fever/temperature and joint pains; breathing OK
- Past medical history: Atopic eczema; asthma (uses blue/SABA inhaler as needed only during flares)
- Medications: Emollients (Diprobase), Dermol in shower; OTC hydrocortisone cream; SABA inhaler PRN; not currently on antihistamines
- Allergies: No known drug allergies
- Family history: Mother with hypothyroidism and migraine
- Social: Lives in London; no exposure changes mentioned
- Vitals/exam: Not recorded in transcript (video visit)
- Labs/imaging: None mentioned

V: Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis: Would present with palpable purpura/petechiae and often pain rather than intense itch; distribution and features here are less consistent, so low likelihood.
Stasis dermatitis: Typically on lower legs with edema/varicosities; distribution (chest/hands/antecubital fossae) argues against this.
I: Secondary bacterial infection (impetiginized eczema): Eczema with skin barrier disruption can become infected (S. aureus); would see weeping, crusting, increased pain or fever—currently absent but cracks present increase risk.

Scabies: Intensely pruritic inflammatory infestation; classically affects finger webs, wrists, waistline, genitals; pruritus often worse at night; distribution and lack of contacts/symptoms lessen likelihood.
Dermatophyte (tinea corporis): Pruritic annular plaques with central clearing; widespread involvement without classic ring morphology makes this less likely.
N: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides): Can mimic eczema with patches/plaques, often chronic, refractory; acute onset over days and atopic history make this unlikely but worth distant consideration if persistent or atypical.
D: Xerosis cutis: Dry skin can exacerbate itch and eczema; seasonal/environmental factors may contribute.
Nutritional deficiency (niacin or zinc): Can cause dermatitis but usually with characteristic patterns and systemic signs; unlikely here.
I2: Allergic contact dermatitis to topical products (e.g., emollients, fragrances, preservatives, lanolin): Could cause/worsen widespread dermatitis; patient denies product changes but sensitization can occur to existing products.
Irritant contact dermatitis (soaps, detergents, frequent washing): Could aggravate eczema; no reported changes but still possible.
Drug eruption: No new systemic medications reported; low likelihood.
C: Ichthyosis vulgaris/atopic diathesis: Congenital keratinization disorder frequently associated with atopy; not documented but could underlie xerosis and eczema severity.
A: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare: Strongly fits pruritic, dry, erythematous rash on flexural surfaces with personal history of eczema and asthma.
Allergic contact dermatitis (type IV hypersensitivity): Can present with pruritic erythematous dermatitis; distribution could be influenced by exposures (hands/arms/chest).
T: Excoriation/lichen simplex chronicus: Secondary to chronic scratching; patient denies scratch marks and thickening, reducing likelihood.
E: Hypothyroidism: Can cause xerosis and pruritus; family history present but patient has no systemic hypothyroid symptoms reported.
Diabetes mellitus: Pruritus and secondary infections possible; no history provided.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic history and distribution (flexural predominance, pruritic, dry, erythematous, cracked skin) in a patient with known eczema and atopic comorbidity (asthma) with acute worsening over days.
supporting_evidence: Personal history of eczema with similar symptoms
Very itchy, dry, sore, red patches; cracked skin
No systemic symptoms (fever/joint pain) suggesting infection
opposing_evidence: OTC hydrocortisone and prior antihistamine provided little relief, suggesting a more severe or refractory flare (but still consistent with eczema)
No thickening/lichenification noted (may reflect acute rather than chronic changes)

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis (superimposed on atopic skin)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Hands/arms/chest involvement could reflect exposure-related dermatitis superimposed on atopic skin; sensitization can occur even without recent product changes.
supporting_evidence: Distribution includes hands and chest—areas commonly exposed to products or irritants
Eczema worsening despite ongoing emollient routine raises possibility of sensitivity to components
Atopic skin barrier dysfunction increases susceptibility to contact dermatitis
opposing_evidence: Patient reports no changes in products or routine
No clear exposure trigger identified in the transcript

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Cracked eczematous skin predisposes to bacterial superinfection, but current lack of weeping, crusting, fever, or marked tenderness lowers probability.
supporting_evidence: Widespread inflamed dermatitis could become secondarily infected
opposing_evidence: Patient describes soreness but not disproportionate pain

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Intense pruritus could suggest scabies, but the distribution and absence of nocturnal predominance, household contacts, or typical sites/signs make it less likely.
opposing_evidence: No involvement of classic sites (finger webs, wrists, genital area) reported
No mention of affected contacts or nocturnal worsening
Rash described as dry, eczematous rather than burrows/papules

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can present with erythematous scaly plaques, but typical extensor surfaces involvement and thick silvery scale/lichenification are not reported; flexural predominance favors eczema.
supporting_evidence: Erythematous, itchy rash can occur in psoriasis
opposing_evidence: Flexural (antecubital) predominance rather than extensor surfaces
No thickened plaques or silvery scale reported
Known history of eczema and atopy better explains presentation
